title: Taif — Praying for Your Enemies' Grandchildren
subtitle: The rejection that became a prayer, and the prayer that became a people
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 3231
Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa), vol. 1 pp. 419-421 (shamela.ws/book/23833/442-444); vol. 2 (the Thaqif delegation, shamela.ws/book/23833/1274)

chapters.heading: The Saddest Day
chapters.body: Ibn Hisham says that after Abu Talib died, Quraysh harmed the Prophet ﷺ more than they had in his uncle's lifetime, and he went alone to Taif seeking support and protection from Thaqif. He came to three brothers, leaders of Thaqif. One said that if Allah had sent him he would be tearing the cloths of the Kaaba; another said the most cutting sentence in the story: 'could Allah not find anyone to send but you?'; the third said he would never speak to him — if he were a messenger he was too great to answer, and if he were lying he was not worth addressing. He asked them to keep it from his people. Then the people of Taif set their fools and slaves on him, who insulted and shouted at him until a crowd gathered, and he was pushed to the wall of a garden belonging to Utba and Shayba, the sons of Rabi'a.
chapters.label: Seerah report

chapters.heading: The Prayer in the Vineyard
chapters.body: He sat in the shade of a grapevine, and the Prophet ﷺ prayed. His prayer is preserved by Ibn Hisham from Ibn Ishaq (it is not in Bukhari, and its chain was not checked here); in this rendering it opens: O Allah, to You I complain of the weakness of my strength, my scarcity of resources and my lowness before the people, O most merciful of the merciful. You are the Lord of the weak, and You are my Lord. To whom do You leave me — to a distant one who meets me with a harsh face, or to an enemy You have given authority over me? If You are not angry with me, I do not mind. Notice what is absent: revenge. Notice what is present: the only question that matters — is Allah angry? Utba and Shayba, watching, were moved by compassion and told their Christian slave Addas to take him a bunch of grapes. The Prophet ﷺ said the name of Allah and ate. Addas said such words are not what people in this land say; the Prophet ﷺ asked where he was from, and Addas said he was a Christian from Nineveh; the Prophet ﷺ said that was the town of the righteous man Jonah son of Matthew, his brother, a prophet as he was. Addas kissed his head, hands and feet. Ibn Hisham does not say that Addas became Muslim: Utba and Shayba told him not to let this man turn him from his religion, since his own was better.
chapters.label: Seerah report

chapters.heading: The Mountains He Refused
chapters.body: Then Jibril came with the angel of the mountains, and the offer was total: say the word, and we will bring the two mountains together on this city. And the Prophet ﷺ answered with the sentence that made Taif's grandchildren his own: 'No — I hope that Allah will bring from their descendants people who will worship Allah alone, and not associate anything with Him' (Bukhari 3231). He had the power of apocalypse in his hand, and he chose the slow power of a dua. Years later, the seerah reports, a delegation from Taif came to him and accepted Islam.

chapters.heading: The Sermon
chapters.body: What do we take from Taif? That the measure of a wound is not its size but what you do with it. Every one of us has a Taif — a rejection, a betrayal, a door slammed in our face by the people we went to in good faith. The Prophet ﷺ did not pretend the rejection was small; Aisha asked whether he had met a day harder than Uhud and he named this one (Bukhari 3231). And he hoped for their descendants. The Qur'an gives the principle: 'Repel [evil] by that [deed] which is better' (41:34). Allahumma, make us people who answer rejection with supplication.
chapters.label: Reflection

chapters.heading: Closing du'a
chapters.body: The Qur'an teaches this du'a for those who come after: 'Our Lord, forgive us and our brothers who preceded us in faith and put not in our hearts [any] resentment toward those who have believed. Our Lord, indeed You are Kind and Merciful' (59:10). Make it your du'a for the one who hurt you and for the children who come after them. Ameen.
chapters.label: Reflection

familyQuestion: Who is your 'Taif' — the person or place that rejected you — and what would praying for their children look like this week?

title: The Weight of One Atom
subtitle: Small things decide everything — 99:7-8 as a life policy
sources: Qur'an 99:1-8
Qur'an 58:1
Sahih al-Bukhari 3467 — the woman who gave a dog water (Abu Hurayrah)
Sahih al-Bukhari 2365 — the woman and the cat (Ibn Umar)
Sahih al-Bukhari 5641 — hardship expiates sins, even a thorn
Sahih Muslim 1914 — the man who moved a thorny branch from the road (Abu Hurayrah)

chapters.heading: The Smallest Verse of the Ledger
chapters.body: 'So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it' (99:7-8). The surah describes the earth shaken and discharging its burdens (99:1-2), and says 'That Day, it will report its news' (99:4). The word is dharrah — a very small thing, translated 'atom'. Not the great sins, not the heroic deeds — the atom. The verse says nothing you do is lost.

chapters.heading: A Bowl of Water
chapters.body: The Prophet ﷺ said that an Israelite prostitute was forgiven for watering a dog dying of thirst (Bukhari 3467). Not a crusade. A little water. And on the other side, he said a woman was put in Hell because of a cat she kept locked until it died of hunger; Allah said to her, 'You neither fed it nor watered it when you locked it up, nor did you set it free to eat the vermin of the earth' (Bukhari 2365). Most of the atoms of your life are invisible to everyone: the thought you resisted, the message you softened, the child you listened to instead of the phone. A reflection: the ones no one saw are the ones only Allah can count.

chapters.heading: The Compounding of Atoms
chapters.body: Consider what small things become. The Qur'an says Nuh remained among his people a thousand years minus fifty (29:14); of the flood Allah says 'We saved him and his family from the great affliction' and 'made his descendants those remaining [on the earth]' (37:76-77). A woman who argued with the Prophet ﷺ about her husband is remembered in the Qur'an: 'Certainly has Allah heard the speech of the one who argues with you ... and directs her complaint to Allah' (58:1). None of them saw the full fruit. So plant atoms: the verse of Qur'an you teach a child, the dua you whisper for a stranger, the thorn you move from the road — the Prophet ﷺ said a man who moved a thorny branch from the path was thanked by Allah and forgiven (Muslim 1914). And he said no hardship, even a thorn's prick, befalls a Muslim without Allah expiating sins by it (Bukhari 5641).

chapters.heading: The Sermon
chapters.body: Make this verse your household policy: in our family, atoms count. A kindness too small to mention is worth mentioning. An apology too small to matter is worth making. A prayer too small to feel is worth praying. The scale that weighs us is accurate beyond any instrument ever made, and its smallest unit is the size of the things we do when nobody is watching. Fill the unseen side of that scale. On the Day when the earth will 'report its news' (99:4), the atoms will speak — make sure yours say something beautiful.
chapters.label: Reflection

chapters.heading: Closing du'a
chapters.body: Our Lord, accept [this] from us. Indeed You are the Hearing, the Knowing (2:127). O Allah, do not let us belittle any good or excuse any wrong because it is small; weigh our atoms with mercy; and write for us a good that no one saw but You. Ameen.
chapters.label: Reflection

familyQuestion: What is one 'atom' — one small good deed — you could make a daily habit starting tomorrow?

title: The Beautiful Patience
subtitle: Ya'qub in Surah Yusuf — grief without despair, hope against the evidence

chapters.heading: The Shirt and the Lie
chapters.body: When Yusuf's brothers brought their father a shirt stained with false blood, Ya'qub said: 'Rather, your souls have enticed you to something, so patience is most fitting. And Allah is the one sought for help against that which you describe' (12:18). Years later, when the news of Binyamin came, he said it again (12:83). The Qur'an gives the picture of his sorrow: 'Oh, my sorrow over Joseph,' and his eyes became white from grief, 'for he was [of that] a suppressor' — kazim, one who holds his grief in (12:84). And still he did not despair of relief from Allah.

chapters.heading: Sabrun Jamil
chapters.body: When the second blow came, the brothers said 'By Allah, you will not cease remembering Joseph until you become fatally ill or become of those who perish' (12:85). Ya'qub answered: 'I only complain of my suffering and my grief to Allah, and I know from Allah that which you do not know' (12:86). He had said earlier, in the phrase the whole religion inherits: 'so patience is most fitting. Perhaps Allah will bring them to me all together. Indeed it is He who is the Knowing, the Wise' (12:83). Patience — and then action: he told his sons to go back and inquire: 'go and find out about Joseph and his brother and despair not of relief from Allah. Indeed, no one despairs of relief from Allah except the disbelieving people' (12:87).

chapters.heading: The Reunion
chapters.body: And then the caravan departed from Egypt, and their father said: 'Indeed, I find the smell of Joseph [and would say that he was alive] if you did not think me weakened in mind' (12:94). They said, 'By Allah, indeed you are in your [same] old error' (12:95). When the bearer of good tidings arrived, he cast the shirt over his face, and he returned seeing (12:96). Yusuf then said: 'O my father, this is the explanation of my vision of before. My Lord has made it reality' (12:100). Sabrun jamil — beautiful patience: grief without despair, hope against the evidence.

chapters.heading: The Sermon
chapters.body: Some of us are holding a stained shirt today — a diagnosis, a betrayal, a son or daughter far from the deen, a door that has stayed closed for years. Ya'qub does not tell you the shirt is not stained. He shows what to do with it: beautiful patience, complaint to Allah alone, and no despair — 'no one despairs of relief from Allah except the disbelieving people' (12:87). Your Yusuf may be nearer than you think. Keep the prayer mat warm.
chapters.label: Reflection

chapters.heading: Closing du'a
chapters.body: The Qur'an records Yusuf's last du'a: 'You are my protector in this world and in the Hereafter. Cause me to die a Muslim and join me with the righteous' (12:101). O Allah, give us beautiful patience, bring back those we have lost to Your obedience, and do not let us despair of relief from You. Ameen.
chapters.label: Reflection

familyQuestion: What is the 'stained shirt' in your family right now — and what would beautiful patience look like, concretely, this week?

title: The First Sermon of the First Caliph
subtitle: Abu Bakr at the Prophet's ﷺ pulpit: the words that held a nation
sources: Ibn Hisham, al-Sira al-Nabawiyya (ed. al-Saqqa), vol. 2 pp. 656, 661 (shamela.ws/book/23833/1393, 1398)
Qur'an 3:144
Sahih al-Bukhari 1399 — the wars against those who refused zakat (Abu Hurayrah)

chapters.heading: Standing in the Shoes of the Prophet
chapters.body: Ibn Hisham gives the scene at the Prophet's ﷺ death. Abu Bakr came to him, kissed his forehead, and said the death Allah had decreed for him he had already tasted. Umar was speaking to the people; Abu Bakr told him to calm down and be quiet, Umar would not, and Abu Bakr spoke to the crowd, who turned to him and stopped listening to Umar. He praised Allah and said: whoever worshipped Muhammad, know that Muhammad has died; and whoever worships Allah, know that Allah is Alive and does not die. Then he recited the verse: 'Muhammad is not but a messenger. [Other] messengers have passed on before him. So if he was to die or be killed, would you turn back on your heels [to unbelief]?' (3:144). The narrator says the people had not realised this verse had been revealed until Abu Bakr recited it that day; Umar said his legs would not hold him and he fell to the ground, and he knew the Prophet ﷺ had died. Ibn Hisham's account then goes to Saqifat Banu Sa'ida, where the Ansar gathered under Sa'd ibn Ubada and the Muhajirun answered them.
chapters.label: Seerah report

chapters.heading: The Charter in Three Sentences
chapters.body: After the pledge, Ibn Hisham gives Abu Bakr's speech to the people: 'I have been appointed over you, and I am not the best of you. If I do right, help me; and if I do wrong, correct me. Truthfulness is trustworthiness; and lying is treachery. The weak among you is strong before me until I restore his right; and the strong among you is weak before me until I take the right from him... Obey me as long as I obey Allah and His Messenger; and if I disobey them, you owe me no obedience.' (The speech goes on: a people who abandon jihad are humbled by Allah, and it ends with the call to rise to prayer.) Four sentences: humility, accountability, the inversion of power toward the weak, and the conditional contract of rule.
chapters.label: Seerah report

chapters.heading: Why It Held
chapters.body: Bukhari reports from Abu Hurayrah that after the Prophet's ﷺ death some of the Arab tribes renounced Islam. Umar questioned fighting them, citing the Prophet's ﷺ words that people are to be fought until they say there is no god but Allah. Abu Bakr answered that he would fight whoever separated prayer from zakat, since zakat is owed from wealth, and that he would fight them even over a young goat that had been paid to the Prophet ﷺ. Umar later said he saw that Allah had opened Abu Bakr's heart to it, and that it was the truth (Sahih al-Bukhari 1399).

chapters.heading: The Sermon
chapters.body: Leaders are measured by the weak they served, and citizens by the wrongs they correct. Ask at your own table this week: who is the 'weak among us' whose right we must restore — and what is the wrong we are positioned to correct? The first caliph's contract is not only for caliphs. It is for every head of a household, every manager, every elder: if I do right, help me; if I do wrong, correct me.
chapters.label: Reflection

chapters.heading: Closing du'a
chapters.body: The youths of the cave prayed: 'Our Lord, grant us from Yourself mercy and prepare for us from our affair right guidance' (18:10). O Allah, guide those entrusted with authority over us, make us people who help when they do right and correct them when they err, and let none of us be a tyrant over the weak. Ameen.
chapters.label: Reflection

familyQuestion: Where in your life are you the 'strong one' before whom the weak must be made strong?

title: The Grammar of Loss
subtitle: Inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un — how to be struck and still stand
sources: Sahih Muslim 918

chapters.heading: The Sentence Everyone Says Wrong
chapters.body: We say it at every death and most of us have never read the verse it comes from in full. In Surah al-Baqarah, Allah says: 'And We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger and a loss of wealth and lives and fruits, but give good tidings to the patient, Who, when disaster strikes them, say, Indeed we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we will return. Those are the ones upon whom are blessings from their Lord and mercy. And it is those who are the [rightly] guided' (2:155-157). The verse is not a funeral phrase. It is a treaty for the living: you WILL be hit — here is the sentence that turns the hit into an address.

chapters.heading: The Mechanics of the Sentence
chapters.body: Look at what the sentence does to the loss. 'Indeed we belong to Allah' — the first half reassigns ownership. Whatever was taken was never ultimately yours; it was a loan from an Owner who lends beautifully and reclaims justly. 'And indeed to Him we will return' — the second half reassigns the destination. The separation is not ending; it is a change of address, and the same Owner holds both addresses. Between the two halves sits the whole of grief — and the sentence does not deny any of it. The Prophet ﷺ wept at his son Ibrahim's death and said: 'the eye weeps and the heart grieves, and we say only what pleases our Lord' (Bukhari 1303). Weeping is not weakness of faith. It is the sign of the loan's value.

chapters.heading: Umm Salama's Version
chapters.body: The Prophet ﷺ taught Umm Salama the completion of the sentence. She reported that he said: if any Muslim who suffers some calamity says what Allah has commanded — 'We belong to Allah and to Him shall we return; O Allah, reward me for my affliction and give me something better than it in exchange' — Allah will give him something better in exchange. When Abu Salama died she said these words, and Allah gave her the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in exchange (Muslim 918). The report does not promise that your replacement will be a prophet's household; it promises that the One who wrote the loss is not finished writing. And the verse itself says that upon those who say it descend blessings from their Lord and mercy, and they are the guided (2:157).

chapters.heading: The Sermon
chapters.body: Learn the sentence the way you learned your name, because the test is promised, not possible: 'We will surely test you.' Then learn Umm Salama's second half, because the reward is attached to the asking. And when the blow comes — it comes to every house — do not perform strength. Weep. Grieve. And then say the treaty out loud, slowly, meaning every word: we belong to Him, and to Him we return. The Owner of both addresses is the same. That sameness is the whole religion.
chapters.label: Reflection

chapters.heading: Closing du'a
chapters.body: Inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un. O Allah, reward us in our afflictions and give us better in exchange (Muslim 918). Our Lord, give us in this world that which is good and in the Hereafter that which is good, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire (2:201). Have mercy on our dead, and console the grieving. Ameen.
chapters.label: Reflection

familyQuestion: Practice the complete dua tonight — including Umm Salama's second half — for a loss you are carrying right now.

title: The Phone in the Hand
subtitle: Attention is worship — the feed as the thief of the one thing you were made to give
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 1036 — time passing quickly, afflictions appearing (Abu Hurayrah)
Sahih al-Bukhari 6018 — speak good or keep silent (Abu Hurayrah)
Sahih al-Bukhari 6412 — health and free time, two blessings many people are deceived into losing (Ibn Abbas)
Sahih Muslim 1914 — the man who removed a thorny branch from the path (Abu Hurayrah)
Sunan Abi Dawud 5082 — the three quls morning and evening (hasan per al-Albani)

chapters.heading: The New Qiblah
chapters.body: The Prophet ﷺ listed among the signs of the Hour that time will pass quickly (Bukhari 1036). A reflection: the infinite scroll is built to take the one currency that matters — your attention — and a believer's attention is part of his worship. The Prophet ﷺ said there are two blessings many people are deceived into losing: health and free time (Bukhari 6412). The Qur'an's warning is older than any device: 'whoever is blinded from remembrance of the Most Merciful - We appoint for him a devil, and he is to him a companion' (43:36). The Qur'an does not say 'avoid technology'; it says do not be blind to remembrance.

chapters.heading: The Fiqh of the Feed
chapters.body: The Prophet's ﷺ rule of speech applies to the screen: 'whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him speak good or remain silent' (Bukhari 6018) — posting included. And the hadith of the man who passed by a thorny branch and put it aside, and Allah thanked him and forgave him (Muslim 1914), points the same way: if a thorn deserves removing from the path, think of what is placed in the path of your children's eyes. A house rule such as no screens at the table is offered here as advice, not as a report from the Prophet ﷺ; the table is where a family gathers.

chapters.heading: The Cure Is Not a Monastery
chapters.body: Withdrawal is not the prescription. The prescription is intention with edges. Give the phone a bedtime an hour before yours. Make the first hour of the day screen-free, and use it for remembrance — the Prophet ﷺ taught the three quls three times in the morning and the evening (Abu Dawud 5082, hasan per al-Albani). Replace, do not just remove: the thirty minutes of scroll you cut tonight can become the first ten verses of Surah al-Kahf, learned over a month — the Prophet ﷺ said whoever memorises them is protected from the Dajjal (Muslim 809). The Qur'an says: 'Your wealth and your children are but a trial, and Allah has with Him a great reward' (64:15) — and your attention is part of what you have been given.

chapters.heading: The Sermon
chapters.body: Hold your phone up and ask it a question: what did you give me today that I will want beside my grave? The feed has no answer; it was built to postpone the question. Tonight, set one boundary the whole family can see — devices sleep in another room, or the table is a no-screen zone — and name it as worship, because guarding your attention for Allah is. Guard the heart as you guard the tongue.
chapters.label: Reflection

chapters.heading: Closing du'a
chapters.body: Our Lord, let not our hearts deviate after You have guided us, and grant us from Yourself mercy. Indeed, You are the Bestower (3:8). O Allah, make us masters of our tools and not their servants; give us time we do not waste and sight we do not squander; and bless our children's eyes and hearts. Ameen.
chapters.label: Reflection

familyQuestion: What is the one screen rule your household could start tonight — and who will enforce it gently?

title: Anxiety and the Medicine of Ta'weel
subtitle: Mental health, the veiled plan, and the dua of the tested
sources: Sahih Muslim 918, 2999
Sahih al-Bukhari 1303, 6369

chapters.heading: Say It Plainly First
chapters.body: A khutbah on anxiety must begin by naming reality: grief, panic, depression, and trauma are real, they are not weakness of faith, and seeking help — a doctor, a counselor, a trusted elder — is not failure of tawakkul. The Prophet ﷺ wept for his son Ibrahim and said: 'the eye weeps and the heart grieves' (Bukhari 1303). Ya'qub's eyes went white from suppressed grief (12:84) — a prophet, grieving like a human, honored in revelation for it. The deen has never asked anyone to pretend the wound is small.

chapters.heading: The Medicine That Is Named
chapters.body: This khutbah calls the medicine, in its own framing, 'deferred interpretation' (ta'weel) — a name for trusting that meanings unfold later, not a Qur'anic prescription for anxiety. 'But perhaps you hate a thing and it is good for you; and perhaps you love a thing and it is bad for you. And Allah Knows, while you know not' (2:216). The angels' own objection at the creation of Adam — 'Will You place upon it one who causes corruption therein and sheds blood?' — was answered: 'Indeed, I know that which you do not know' (2:30). A reflection: anxiety is often the pain of a story whose last chapters we have not been shown. The Prophet ﷺ said: 'amazing is the affair of the believer — all of it is good for him' (Muslim 2999).

chapters.heading: The Dua for the 3am Ceiling
chapters.body: The Prophet ﷺ used to say: 'O Allah, I seek refuge with You from worry and grief, from incapacity and laziness, from cowardice and miserliness, from being heavily in debt and from being overpowered by men' (Bukhari 6369, from Anas). And he taught the dua of the afflicted: 'We belong to Allah and to Him shall we return; O Allah, reward me for my affliction and give me something better than it in exchange' (Muslim 918). These duas do not shame the asker. Combine them with the means: sleep, movement, food, community, and when the load is heavy, a doctor or counsellor. Tawakkul does not cancel the means.

chapters.heading: The Sermon
chapters.body: To the anxious believer reading this at 3am: racing hearts are not a sign of weak faith. Say the dua slowly — it fits inside one breath. Text one person today, not to perform strength but to be accompanied. And hold the ta'weel like a handrail: the chapter you are in is not the ending. Allah does not charge a soul except [with that within] its capacity (2:286).
chapters.label: Reflection

chapters.heading: Closing du'a
chapters.body: Our Lord, do not impose blame upon us if we have forgotten or erred. Our Lord, and burden us not with that which we have no ability to bear. And pardon us; and forgive us; and have mercy upon us (2:286). O Allah, remove from us worry and grief, and send us calm and company. Ameen.
chapters.label: Reflection

familyQuestion: Who in your circle is carrying anxiety silently right now — and could you send them this sermon tonight?

title: The Quiet Chain
subtitle: Debt, riba, and the spending self in a buy-now civilization
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 832 — the Prophet's ﷺ refuge from debt: a man in debt speaks and lies, promises and breaks his promise (Aisha)
Sahih Muslim 1598 — the one who takes interest, the one who pays it, the one who records it, the two witnesses (Jabir)
Sunan Ibn Majah 2443 — 'Give the worker his wages before his sweat dries' (sahih per al-Albani and Zubair Ali Za'i of Darussalam)
Sahih al-Bukhari 2305 — the best of you are the best in repaying (Abu Hurayrah)
Sahih al-Bukhari 1410 — charity from lawful earnings, even a date (Abu Hurayrah)
Jami` at-Tirmidhi 3563 — the dua for freedom from debt (hasan per al-Albani)

chapters.heading: The Warning That Has Not Expired
chapters.body: The Prophet ﷺ used to seek refuge in his prayer from debt, and when he was asked why, he said: a man in debt speaks and lies, promises and breaks his promise (Bukhari 832, from Aisha). And the Qur'an's warning on interest stands: 'But Allah has permitted trade and has forbidden interest ... But whoever returns to [dealing in interest or usury] - those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide eternally therein' (2:275). The Qur'an also says 'fear Allah and give up what remains [due to you] of interest, if you should be believers' (2:278). A reflection: buy-now-pay-later has made borrowing easy to the point where we stop noticing it.

chapters.heading: The Scale Weighs the Contract
chapters.body: Jabir reported that the Prophet ﷺ cursed the one who takes interest, the one who pays it, the one who records it and the two witnesses, and said 'They are all equal' (Muslim 1598). Which modern financial arrangements count as riba, and whether necessity ever permits a particular contract (such as a home loan in a land where no alternative exists), are questions on which scholars give differing rulings; this khutbah does not give a fatwa, and you should ask a trusted scholar about your own contract. What no one disputes is the direction: reduce what you owe, and prefer the lawful. 'Allah does not charge a soul except [with that within] its capacity' (2:286) is a promise of sufficiency, not a permission to sign.

chapters.heading: The Other Debt: What We Owe
chapters.body: There is another debt: what we owe to people. 'Give the worker his wages before his sweat dries' (Ibn Majah 2443, sahih per al-Albani and per Zubair Ali Za'i of Darussalam). The Prophet ﷺ once owed a man a camel of a certain age, and when none of that age could be found he told his companions to give him a better one, saying that the best of you are the best in repaying (Bukhari 2305). Give before you are asked, in one small amount weekly: the Prophet ﷺ said that whoever gives in charity the equal of a date from lawful earnings, Allah takes it in His right hand and enlarges its reward (Bukhari 1410). And make the intention on every lawful purchase: provision, not anesthesia.

chapters.heading: The Sermon
chapters.body: Do one thing this week with your finances that no algorithm will reward: list every debt and take one step — a call, a plan, a consultation with a scholar or advisor — toward its end. Then teach one child in your house the dua Ali reported the Prophet ﷺ taught: 'O Allah, suffice me with Your lawful against Your unlawful, and enrich me by Your bounty from all besides You' (Tirmidhi 3563, hasan per al-Albani). The chain is quiet until it isn't. Break one link while the breaking is easy.
chapters.label: Reflection

chapters.heading: Closing du'a
chapters.body: Allahumma ikfini bi-halalika 'an haramik, wa aghnini bi-fadlika 'amman siwak — O Allah, suffice me with Your lawful against Your unlawful, and enrich me by Your bounty from all besides You (Tirmidhi 3563, hasan per al-Albani). Our Lord, give us in this world that which is good and in the Hereafter that which is good (2:201). Free us from debt and from fear of poverty. Ameen.
chapters.label: Reflection

familyQuestion: Which debt — financial or personal — could you take one concrete step toward this week?

title: Loneliness in the Crowd
subtitle: Five hundred friends, no one to call — rebuilding the majlis
sources: Qur'an 12:87

chapters.heading: The Epidemic With No App
chapters.body: We live in the most connected loneliness in human history. The feeds are full and the houses are quiet; the followers are counted and the visitors are not. Yet the Prophet ﷺ described the believers' bond with each other: 'a faithful believer to a faithful believer is like the bricks of a wall, enforcing each other' (Bukhari 481); the Prophet ﷺ described the believers in their mercy and love for each other as one body, so that if one part ails the rest respond (Bukhari 6011). The Qur'an describes the people of Paradise as brothers 'on thrones facing each other' (15:47) — the afterlife is pictured, deliberately, as face-to-face company. The feed is not company. It is the memory of faces.

chapters.heading: The Three Doors Back
chapters.body: The sunnah offers three doors out of loneliness, all small enough to open this week. The neighbor's door: the Prophet ﷺ said that whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day should honor his neighbor (Bukhari 6018) — begin with salaam and a plate, not an apology for the past. The mosque's door: the rows of prayer are the last standing weekly gathering where age, income, and language sit shoulder to shoulder — the Prophet ﷺ said that the prayer in congregation is twenty-seven times superior to the prayer offered by a person alone (Bukhari 645). And the family's door: the parent you call weekly, the sibling you forgive, the cousin you visit — 'whoever desires an expansion in his sustenance and age should keep good relations with his kith and kin' (Bukhari 2067). Loneliness is a debt the whole community owes back; start paying it on someone else's behalf too.

chapters.heading: The Permission to Be Alone
chapters.body: A word for the introverts and the wounded: solitude is not the disease; isolation is. The Prophet ﷺ took the cave of Hira; Maryam withdrew to the eastern chamber; 'devote yourself to Him with [complete] devotion' (73:8) presumes a room. The test is the direction of the solitude — toward Allah or away from people? If your alone hours refill you for the rows, the neighbor, the family table, they are the mosque's anteroom. If they only deepen the echo, answer the echo with one invitation this month — the majlis begins with a kettle, not a program. And if the loneliness has become despair, treat it like any other chest pain: tell someone today. 'No one despairs of relief from Allah except the disbelieving people' (12:87) was said to a grieving father — and it is said to you.

chapters.heading: The Sermon
chapters.body: This week, convert one digital habit into a physical one. The fifteen minutes you would spend watching a stranger's meal, spend eating with a real person — even one. The believers are like the bricks of a wall. Be, this week, one brick in someone else's wall. The ummah was always built face to face.
chapters.label: Reflection

chapters.heading: Closing du'a
chapters.body: Zakariyya called: 'My Lord, do not leave me alone [with no heir], while You are the best of inheritors' (21:89). O Allah, never leave us alone: give us righteous companions, open doors to those who knock, and be with those who are lonely tonight. Ameen.
chapters.label: Reflection

familyQuestion: Who is the loneliest person you know — and what would 'pulling out a chair' for them look like this week?

title: Raising Children in the Feed
subtitle: Every child is born on fitrah — but the house sets the weather
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 1385 — every child is born on fitrah (Abu Hurayrah)
Sahih al-Bukhari 709 — shortening the prayer at a child's cry (Anas)
Sahih al-Bukhari 6247 — greeting children (Anas)
Sahih al-Bukhari 454 — Aisha watching the Ethiopians (Aisha)
Sahih al-Bukhari 143 — dua for Ibn Abbas
Jami` at-Tirmidhi 2378 — 'A man is upon the religion of his friend' (hasan per al-Albani)
Qur'an 25:74

chapters.heading: The Fitrah and the Soil
chapters.body: The Prophet ﷺ said that every child is born on fitrah, and his parents make him a Jew, a Christian or a Magian (Bukhari 1385). Read that hadith twice, because it places the first responsibility for a child's religion with the home. A reflection: the mosque gets the child an hour a week; the house gets the rest, and the house now competes with commercial screens for the same child. What the house watches, eats, argues over and laughs at becomes the weather the child grows in.

chapters.heading: The Sunnah With Children
chapters.body: The Prophet ﷺ said: 'When I start the prayer I intend to prolong it, but on hearing the cries of a child, I cut short the prayer because I know that the cries of the child will incite its mother's passions' (Bukhari 709). Anas passed a group of boys, greeted them, and said the Prophet ﷺ used to do so (Bukhari 6247). Aisha watched the Ethiopians play in the mosque while the Prophet ﷺ screened her with his cloak (Bukhari 454). A reflection: children learn from what they see more than from what they are told, so pray where they can see you, and apologize when you are wrong.

chapters.heading: Five Small Laws for the House
chapters.body: Five small laws for the house, offered as advice rather than as reports. First: the child hears the Qur'an daily in the parent's own voice. Second: one family meal, no screens, most days. Third: the dua over each child by name, aloud — the Prophet ﷺ made dua for Ibn Abbas, 'O Allah! Make him a learned scholar in religion' (Bukhari 143). Fourth: admit the gap between your preaching and your practice. Fifth: choose the house's influences like friends — the Prophet ﷺ said 'A man is upon the religion of his friend, so let one of you look at whom he befriends' (Tirmidhi 2378, hasan per al-Albani).
chapters.label: Reflection

chapters.heading: The Sermon
chapters.body: To the parent who feels behind — the feed shows you curated children in curated homes, and your house is loud and behind schedule: the Prophet's ﷺ measure was not the child's trophies but the parent's consistency. Start with one law from the five, tonight. And to every adult reading: somewhere near you is a child whose soil is being set by someone tired. Be the aunt, the uncle, the neighbor whose salaam and whose example plant one seed the parents cannot plant. The fitrah is in every child. The weather is ours to make.
chapters.label: Reflection

chapters.heading: Closing du'a
chapters.body: The Qur'an teaches the parents' du'a: 'Our Lord, grant us from among our wives and offspring comfort to our eyes and make us an example for the righteous' (25:74). And Ibrahim's: 'My Lord, make me an establisher of prayer, and [many] from my descendants. Our Lord, and accept my supplication' (14:40). O Allah, guide our children, protect them, and make us worthy of them. Ameen.
chapters.label: Reflection

familyQuestion: Which of the five house laws will you start this week — and which one are you already breaking in front of them?

title: Built to Rest
subtitle: Burnout, the right to stop, and Friday as a standing appointment
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 676 — the Prophet ﷺ serving his family (Aisha)
Sunan Abi Dawud 2578 — the Prophet's ﷺ race with Aisha (sahih per al-Albani)
Jami` at-Tirmidhi 2344 — reliance on Allah like the birds (sahih per al-Albani; isnad hasan per Zubair Ali Za'i)
Sahih al-Bukhari 1968 — 'your body has a right over you' (Abu Juhayfa)

chapters.heading: The Wage of the Overworked Self
chapters.body: The modern economy sells exhaustion as virtue. Into that noise the Qur'an speaks: 'And out of His mercy He made for you the night and the day that you may rest therein and [by day] seek from His bounty and [that] perhaps you will be grateful' (28:73). Rest is one of the two halves the day was built from. A reflection: the five prayers punctuate the day, and 'prayer prohibits immorality and wrongdoing, and the remembrance of Allah is greater' (29:45). Salman told Abu al-Darda, who was fasting by day and standing by night: 'Your Lord has a right on you, your soul has a right on you, and your family has a right on you; so give the rights of all those who have a right on you' — and the Prophet ﷺ said: Salman has spoken the truth (Bukhari 1968).

chapters.heading: The Prophet's ﷺ Pace
chapters.body: Look at the Prophet's ﷺ actual pace. Aisha said that in his house he kept himself busy serving his family, and when the time for prayer came he went out for it (Bukhari 676). He raced Aisha (Abu Dawud 2578, sahih per al-Albani). And he taught reliance: 'If you were to rely upon Allah with the required reliance, then He would provide for you just as a bird is provided for: it goes out in the morning empty, and returns full' (Tirmidhi 2344, sahih per al-Albani). The bird still goes out; it just does not carry the world on its wing.

chapters.heading: Friday: The Appointed Stop
chapters.body: Allah says: 'O you who have believed, when [the adhan] is called for the prayer on the day of Jumu'ah [Friday], then proceed to the remembrance of Allah and leave trade. That is better for you, if you only knew' (62:9). Then: 'And when the prayer has been concluded, disperse within the land and seek from the bounty of Allah' (62:10). Jumu'ah is therefore a stop in the day, not a legal day off: the rest of Friday is open for work after the prayer. The command to leave trade applies to those obliged to attend, and scholars differ on details such as which call it begins at; ask your imam. A reflection: a week with a fixed stop in it has a rhythm.

chapters.heading: The Sermon
chapters.body: Audit your last month: how many prayers were prayed on time and how many were 'caught up'? Restore one boundary this week — a stop, Jumu'ah kept in full, a night's sleep defended — and name it what it is: giving each right its due, as Salman said. You were not made to be used up.
chapters.label: Reflection

chapters.heading: Closing du'a
chapters.body: Moses asked: 'My Lord, expand for me my breast [with assurance] and ease for me my task' (20:25-26). O Allah, put barakah in our time, give us rest that strengthens us for worship, and forgive us for the times we mistook busyness for devotion. Ameen.
chapters.label: Reflection

familyQuestion: What is one 'stop' — a boundary with work or screens — you will defend this week as worship?

title: The News That Ate the Heart
subtitle: Doomscrolling, the dying art of silence, and guarding the chest
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 52 — the morsel of flesh (Nu'man ibn Bashir)
Sahih al-Bukhari 6306 — sayyid al-istighfar (Shaddad ibn Aws)
Sahih al-Bukhari 6464 — the most beloved deed is the most consistent (Aisha)
Sahih Muslim 55 — the religion is sincere advice (Tamim al-Dari)
Sunan Abi Dawud 775 — seeking refuge from Shaytan in the night prayer (sahih per al-Albani)

chapters.heading: A Heart Designed Small
chapters.body: The news economy rents your attention to the worst events of every country, simultaneously, forever. A reflection: the heart was not built for the whole world's grief at once. The Prophet ﷺ said: 'The religion is sincerity' — to Allah, His Book, His Messenger, the leaders of the Muslims and their common people (Muslim 55, from Tamim al-Dari). That is a scope. Concern without scope turns into consumption.

chapters.heading: The Doom Loop Is a Door
chapters.body: The Qur'an speaks of the whisperer who 'whispers [evil] into the breasts of mankind - from among the jinn and mankind' (114:5-6). A reflection: the doom loop is not information; it is a rhythm — alarm, refresh, alarm. The counter-practice is in the sunnah: 'the most beloved deed to Allah is the most consistent, even if small' (Bukhari 6464). Set the rhythm before the feed sets it: morning remembrance before headlines (Bukhari 6306, sayyid al-istighfar), a fixed news window rather than an ambient one, and seeking refuge in Allah from Shaytan when the chest tightens — the Prophet ﷺ sought refuge in his night prayer (Abu Dawud 775, sahih per al-Albani). Guard the chest and the news shrinks to its proper size.

chapters.heading: Compassion Needs a Vessel
chapters.body: This is not a sermon against caring. The ummah's crises deserve tears, duas and real help. A reflection: compassion without a vessel spills into despair, and the Qur'an forbids despair of Allah's relief (12:87). Build the vessel: give sadaqah on a schedule so help is systematic, not emotional; make dua by name for the causes you follow; then close the app and do one local good deed. The heart that helps its neighbour is doing more for the world than the heart that carries every headline.

chapters.heading: The Sermon
chapters.body: Try the seven-day perimeter: one fixed news window, twice daily, outside prayer times and the first hour of the morning. The Prophet ﷺ said: 'there is a morsel of flesh in the body, if it is sound the whole body is sound, and if it is corrupted the whole body is corrupted — it is the heart' (Bukhari 52). Watch what happens to your chest, and give the heart back to the remembrance of Allah and the faces in your actual room.
chapters.label: Reflection

chapters.heading: Closing du'a
chapters.body: The Qur'an teaches: 'My Lord, I seek refuge in You from the incitements of the devils. And I seek refuge in You, my Lord, lest they be present with me' (23:97-98). O Allah, guard our hearts from what we do not need to carry, help those who suffer, and make our concern turn into du'a and good deeds. Ameen.
chapters.label: Reflection

familyQuestion: What would your news intake look like if the heart's health set the rules instead of the algorithm?

title: For the One Who Is Tired
subtitle: Rest is not weakness
sources: Qur'an 94:5-6
Qur'an 2:286
Sahih al-Bukhari 6464 — the most beloved deed is the most consistent (Aisha)
Sahih al-Bukhari 1968 — your body has a right over you (Abu Juhayfa)
Sahih al-Bukhari 5641 — hardship expiates sins (Abu Sa'id and Abu Hurayrah)

chapters.heading: The Tired Believer
chapters.body: Fatigue is not the absence of faith; sometimes it is the exhaust of faithfulness. You have been carrying people, bills, prayers and patience — and you feel it. Salman told his brother Abu al-Darda: 'Your Lord has a right on you, your soul has a right on you, and your family has a right on you; so give the rights of all those who have a right on you' — and the Prophet ﷺ said: Salman has spoken the truth (Bukhari 1968). Rest, given its due, is one of those rights.

chapters.heading: The Promise
chapters.body: 'For indeed, with hardship [will be] ease. Indeed, with hardship [will be] ease' (94:5-6). The ease is stated with the hardship. And 'Allah does not charge a soul except [with that within] its capacity' (2:286). The Prophet ﷺ said that no fatigue, disease, sorrow, sadness, hurt or distress befalls a Muslim, even the prick of a thorn, but that Allah expiates some of his sins by it (Bukhari 5641). Your tiredness is seen and counted.

chapters.heading: The Practice
chapters.body: Do one small thing well today: one prayer on time, one kind word, one honest hour of rest without guilt. 'The most beloved deeds to Allah are the most consistent, even if small' (Bukhari 6464). Small, steady, and sincere — that is the whole religion.

chapters.heading: The Sermon
chapters.body: Whoever you are carrying today — a family, a business, a secret struggle — know that Allah knows the weight of it. Tonight, hand Him the load you were never meant to carry alone, and sleep. Allah does not charge a soul except with what is within its capacity (2:286); a rested believer prays, works and cares for others better than an exhausted one.
chapters.label: Reflection

chapters.heading: Closing du'a
chapters.body: Our Lord, pour upon us patience and plant firmly our feet (2:250). Our Lord, and burden us not with that which we have no ability to bear (2:286). O Allah, give us rest that restores, work that is blessed, and the strength to do the small things consistently. Ameen.
chapters.label: Reflection

familyQuestion: What load could you hand to Allah tonight that you have been carrying alone?

title: The Load She Carries — A Khutbah for the Unseen
subtitle: When the world sees the output and not the weight, the deen names the burden and crowns the bearer
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 3 — the first revelation and Khadijah's words (Aisha)
Sahih al-Bukhari 676 — the Prophet ﷺ serving his family (Aisha)
Sunan at-Tirmidhi 1162 — the best of you are the best to their women (hasan sahih per al-Tirmidhi and al-Albani)
Sahih Muslim 442 — do not prevent women from the mosque (Ibn Umar)
Sahih al-Bukhari 1303

chapters.heading: The Invisible Load
chapters.body: There is a weight that does not appear on any scale. The mother who wakes before dawn to pack lunches and make du'a over each child's head. The daughter who translates medical forms for parents who built her future in a language they never fully learned. The wife who carries the emotional weather of the household — who notices when the husband's silence means worry, when the child's grades are slipping, when the sister-in-law needs a call. The working woman who codes, teaches, heals, or leads, and then comes home to a second shift no paycheck names. The world calls this 'having it all.' The body often calls it exhaustion. And the heart sometimes whispers: does anyone see?
chapters.label: Reflection

chapters.heading: The Prophet's Household
chapters.body: The first revelation broke the Prophet ﷺ in the cave of Hira — shook him until he trembled, made him fear for his life. He ran home not to a fortress but to a wife, and his first words were: 'Cover me, cover me.' And Khadijah, radiyallahu anha, did not ask for a business plan or a timeline. She covered him. She believed him. She took him to her cousin Waraqah, who confirmed the truth. Her first words to him that night were that Allah would never disgrace him, because he kept the ties of kinship, bore the burdens of the weak and honored his guests (Bukhari 3). The hadith shows Khadijah's support in the hardest hour of the first revelation. And he was part of his household's work: Aisha said he used to keep himself busy serving his family, and when it was time for prayer he went out for it (Bukhari 676). And he said: 'The most complete of believers in faith are those with the best character, and the best of you are those who are best to their wives' (Tirmidhi 1162, hasan per Darussalam). The standard is not perfection; it is presence, kindness, and the refusal to take the unseen for granted.

chapters.heading: The Weight Is Seen
chapters.body: The Qur'an does not divide virtue by gender; it doubles it: 'Indeed, the Muslim men and Muslim women, the believing men and believing women, the obedient men and obedient women, the truthful men and truthful women, the patient men and patient women, the humble men and humble women, the charitable men and charitable women, the fasting men and fasting women, the men who guard their private parts and the women who do so, and the men who remember Allah often and the women who do so — for them Allah has prepared forgiveness and a great reward' (33:35). Ten pairs, twenty categories, one reward. And again: 'Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while he is a believer — We will surely cause him to live a good life, and We will surely give them their reward according to the best of what they used to do' (16:97). The load you carry in secret — the meal made when you were empty, the patience practiced when you were furious, the prayer whispered when no one was listening — is not invisible to the One who matters. Allah says: 'Never will I allow to be lost the work of [any] worker among you, whether male or female; you are of one another' (3:195). To the woman reading this who feels unseen: Allah does not lose track of your work.

chapters.heading: The Sermon
chapters.body: To the men in this community: the women around you are not 'having it all.' They are carrying it all, and some of them are carrying you too. The question is not what they should do less of; it is what you should do more of. Take one task off her plate this week without being asked. Notice the labor that has become invisible because it is constant. And name it — not with flowers once a year, but with consistent presence. To the women: your exhaustion is not a failure of faith. The Prophet ﷺ wept for his son and said 'the eye weeps and the heart grieves' (Bukhari 1303) . Your tears are not weakness; they are the overflow of a heart that has been holding too much. Ask for help. Delegate. Rest. The deen that commands kindness to neighbors begins with kindness to yourself. And to the community: build structures that see women — not as tokens on boards or decorations at events, but as whole people with bodies that tire and hearts that need the same majlis the men need. The Prophet ﷺ said: do not prevent the maid-servants of Allah from going to the mosque (Muslim 442, from Ibn Umar). Allahumma, make us a community where no load is carried alone, and where the unseen labor is seen, honored, and shared.
chapters.label: Reflection

chapters.heading: Closing du'a
chapters.body: Ibrahim called: 'My Lord, make me an establisher of prayer, and [many] from my descendants. Our Lord, and accept my supplication. Our Lord, forgive me and my parents and the believers the Day the account is established' (14:40-41). O Allah, ease the load of every mother, daughter, wife and sister, see their work, and teach us to share it. Ameen.
chapters.label: Reflection

familyQuestion: What load is someone in your household carrying invisibly — and what would taking one piece of it look like this week?

title: The Door That Opens With the Pain
subtitle: Sabr is not waiting for the storm to pass — it is learning to stand in the rain
sources: Qur'an 94:5-6
Qur'an 12:86
Sahih al-Bukhari 1283 — patience is at the first stroke of calamity (Anas)
Sahih al-Bukhari 2444 — help your brother, oppressor or oppressed (Anas)

chapters.heading: The Instruction Is a Sentence Long
chapters.body: Allah does not give the patient a chapter of instructions. He gives them one sentence and repeats it: 'Indeed, Allah is with the patient' (2:153). Not with the strong, not with the finished, not with the ones who have already recovered — with the patient. The ones still standing in it. If you are in a season where the dua has not landed yet, you have not been skipped. You have been addressed.

chapters.heading: Ayyub Asked by Name
chapters.body: Ayyub did not summarize his suffering. He named it: 'Indeed, adversity has touched me, and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful' (21:83). He brought the wound and the praise in the same breath. The answer came: Allah removed what afflicted him (21:84), and in Surah Sad the instruction to move is given: strike the ground with your foot — here is a cool bath and a drink (38:41-42). Notice — the relief required his participation. Patience is not paralysis. It is staying in place until Allah says move, and then moving.

chapters.heading: With Hardship, Ease — Twice
chapters.body: The shortest surah in the book makes the loudest promise, and then says it again: 'For indeed, with hardship [will be] ease. Indeed, with hardship [will be] ease' (94:5-6). The verse states it twice; you may not see the ease yet, but it does not need your sight to be real.

chapters.heading: What Patience Is Not
chapters.body: Patience is not pretending it doesn't hurt. Ya'qub said 'I only complain of my suffering and my grief to Allah' (12:86) — complaint and patience rode together. Patience is not passivity — Ayyub was told to strike. And it is not silent endurance of injustice: the Prophet ﷺ said, help your brother whether he is an oppressor or oppressed, and explained that helping an oppressor is to stop him from oppressing (Bukhari 2444). A reflection: patience is the refusal to let the pain write the ending.

chapters.heading: Closing du'a
chapters.body: The sorcerers of Pharaoh prayed: 'Our Lord, pour upon us patience and let us die as Muslims [in submission to You]' (7:126). O Allah, give us patience at the first stroke of calamity, relief in Your time, and hearts that complain only to You. Ameen.
chapters.label: Reflection

familyQuestion: What is one hard thing in our house right now that we could face 'with hardship comes ease' about together this week?

title: The Increase Clause
subtitle: Gratitude is not a mood — it is a contract with an increase written into it
sources: Qur'an 14:7
Qur'an 16:18
Qur'an 39:7
Qur'an 2:152
Sahih al-Bukhari 1303
Sahih al-Bukhari 6312 — the dua on waking (Hudhayfa)
Jami` at-Tirmidhi 3458 — the dua after eating (hasan per al-Albani)

chapters.heading: A Verse That Sounds Like a Business Deal
chapters.body: 'If you are grateful, I will surely increase you' (14:7). Allah states it as a promise. Gratitude here is not a feeling that visits; it is a practice you perform — counting, naming, saying alhamdulillah when the count is easy and when it is not. And the promise attached to it is not vague blessing. It is increase. Of what? The verse leaves it open, which means it covers everything the word can hold.

chapters.heading: You Cannot Count Them — That Is the Point
chapters.body: 'If you should count the favors of Allah, you could not enumerate them' (16:18). This is not a challenge; it is a description of your life. Breath you didn't earn. A heart beating without your management. People who would answer your call at 3am. The very existence of the Quran in your language. Gratitude begins the moment you stop waiting for the big thing and start counting the uncountable small ones.

chapters.heading: Gratitude in a Hard Season
chapters.body: Can shukr and grief live in the same chest? Ask the Prophet ﷺ, who wept at the death of his son Ibrahim (Bukhari 1303) and said the eyes weep and the heart grieves, and we say only what pleases our Lord. Gratitude is not the denial of pain; it is the refusal to let pain be the only witness. Even in loss, the believer can say: You gave, You took, You alone remain praised.

chapters.heading: The Smallest Unit of Gratitude
chapters.body: If the practice feels heavy, start at the smallest unit: alhamdulillah after eating and after rising (the Prophet ﷺ taught on waking: 'Praise is to Allah who gave us life after He had caused us to die, and to Him is the resurrection' — Bukhari 6312; and after eating: 'Praise is to Allah who fed me this and provided it for me without any might or power from me' — Tirmidhi 3458, hasan per al-Albani). Each one is a small act of thanks, and Allah has promised increase to the grateful (14:7). 'So remember Me; I will remember you. And be grateful to Me and do not deny Me' (2:152). He asks to be counted. That is all. Begin tonight, before sleep, with three.

chapters.heading: Closing du'a
chapters.body: Sulayman prayed: 'My Lord, enable me to be grateful for Your favor which You have bestowed upon me and upon my parents and to do righteousness of which You approve. And admit me by Your mercy into [the ranks of] Your righteous servants' (27:19). O Allah, make us among the grateful, and let our thanks be in deeds as well as words. Ameen.
chapters.label: Reflection

familyQuestion: At dinner this week, what are three small favors each of us can name that we never earned and could never count?

title: How a Friday Khutbah Is Built
subtitle: What the hadith report of the Prophet's ﷺ khutbah — and where the schools differ
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 928 — two khutbahs with a sitting between them (Ibn Umar)
Sahih Muslim 862 — he delivered it standing, sat, and stood again (Jabir ibn Samura)
Sahih Muslim 868 — the Prophet's ﷺ opening praise and testimony (Ibn Abbas)
Sahih Muslim 867 — he praised Allah and extolled Him; the best speech is the Book of Allah (Jabir ibn Abdullah)
Sahih Muslim 873 — he recited Surah Qaf on the pulpit (Umm Hisham)
Sahih Muslim 869 — a short khutbah and a long prayer (Ammar)
Sahih al-Bukhari 934 and Sahih Muslim 851 — listening to the khutbah (Abu Hurayrah)

chapters.heading: What He Did
chapters.body: Ibn Umar reported that the Prophet ﷺ used to deliver two khutbahs and sit in between them (Bukhari 928). Jabir ibn Samura said he delivered the sermon standing, then sat, then stood again, and that whoever told you he delivered it sitting had lied (Muslim 862). He recited Qur'an and exhorted the people (Muslim 862). Umm Hisham said she learned Surah Qaf from the tongue of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who recited it every Friday on the pulpit (Muslim 873).

chapters.heading: Praise, Testimony and Blessings
chapters.body: Ibn Abbas reported the Prophet's ﷺ words: 'Praise is due to Allah, we praise Him and ask His help; he whom Allah guides aright there is none to lead him astray, and he who is led astray there is none to guide him; and I bear testimony that there is no god but Allah, He is One, having no partner, and that Muhammad is His servant and messenger' (Muslim 868). Jabir reported that when he gave the sermon he praised Allah as He deserves and then said that the best of speech is the Book of Allah (Muslim 867). Sending blessings on the Prophet ﷺ is commanded in the Qur'an: 'Indeed, Allah confers blessing upon the Prophet, and His angels [ask Him to do so]. O you who have believed, ask [Allah to confer] blessing upon him and ask [Allah to grant him] peace' (33:56).

chapters.heading: Short and Direct
chapters.body: Ammar reported the Prophet ﷺ saying that the lengthening of a man's prayer and the shortness of his sermon is a sign of his understanding, so lengthen the prayer and shorten the sermon (Muslim 869). Jabir said that when he gave the sermon his eyes reddened and his voice rose, as if he were warning of an enemy (Muslim 867). The listener has duties too: Abu Hurayrah reported that if you tell your companion to be quiet while the imam is giving the khutbah you have spoken idly (Bukhari 934; Muslim 851), and Allah says to leave trade at the call to the prayer (62:9).

chapters.heading: Where the Schools Differ
chapters.body: The schools differ on which parts of the khutbah are obligatory and which recommended — for example whether the praise, the blessings on the Prophet ﷺ, a verse of Qur'an, the advice to fear Allah and a dua for the believers are each required, how many are required, and whether the khutbah must be in Arabic. This app does not state a ruling. If you are the khatib, follow your school and your imam, and take the hadith above as the model.

chapters.heading: How the App's Khutbahs Are Built
chapters.body: The khutbahs in this app are outlines of reminders, not complete Friday sermons. Each gives sourced material for the reminder and ends with a closing du'a. A khatib would open with the praise and testimony and blessings on the Prophet ﷺ as above, then give the reminder, then close with du'a. Everything in the reminders is labelled as established, interpretive, a report or a reflection, so that a reflection is never read as a hadith.
chapters.label: Reflection

familyQuestion: The Prophet ﷺ's khutbah was short, began with praise and testimony, and carried a reminder. What is one reminder you could give your family in three sentences this Friday?
